case_studies.title: A Gateway Architecture for Enterprise MCP Authentication: Unifying Heterogeneous Auth, Identity Delegation, and the User / Non-User Persona Problem
case_studies.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has become the de-facto interface for connecting LLM agents to enterprise tools, and adoption has been explosive: within a year, large organizations went from zero to dozens of internally built MCP servers. That speed created a governance crisis. Each team implemented authentication independently -- some with no auth, some with API keys, some with full OAuth -- producing a fragmented landscape with no consistent way to authorize callers, track who did what, or offboard a departing employee across the fleet. This paper reports an industry deployment that resolve
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of fragmented authentication in enterprise Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, by building a gateway architecture that unifies authentication, identity delegation, and user management. The result is a more secure and governable MCP ecosystem. The gateway architecture provides a consistent way to authorize callers and manage user identities across the fleet.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage MCP servers, here is what to do: implement a unified gateway architecture to standardize authentication and identity delegation, review your current authentication methods to identify gaps, and prioritize deployment of the gateway to improve security and governance.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper introduces a novel architecture for enterprise MCP authentication, relevant to IT infrastructure management and security. While novelty is moderate, real-world impact is high due to its direct effect on authentication, identity delegation, and user/non-user persona management in enterprise environments. Monetisation potential is limited as it doesn't propose a new business model but rather a technical solution. Low_signal: false

case_studies.title: AgentSOC: A Multi-Layer Agentic AI Framework for Security Operations Automation
case_studies.abstract: Security Operations Centers (SOCs) increasingly encounter difficulties in correlating heterogeneous alerts, interpreting multi-stage attack progressions, and selecting safe and effective response actions. This study introduces AgentSOC, a multi-layered agentic AI framework that enhances SOC automation by integrating perception, anticipatory reasoning, and risk-based action planning. The proposed architecture consolidates several layers of abstraction to provide a single operational loop to support normalizing alerts, enriching context, generating hypotheses, validating structural feasibility,
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of correlating and responding to security alerts in Security Operations Centers, by building a multi-layered AI framework called AgentSOC, which resulted in enhanced automation of security operations. The framework integrates perception, reasoning, and risk-based action planning to improve response to security threats. This is relevant to IT security work in managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage a Security Operations Center, here is what to do: review your current alert correlation and response processes, assess the potential for integrating AgentSOC or similar AI frameworks, and evaluate the benefits of enhanced automation for your organization's security posture.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High novelty due to mention of agentic AI and multi-layered architecture. Direct relevance to security operations automation. High 90-day value due to specific mentions of automating SOC processes. The proposed framework has the potential to improve security operations, and an IT engineer could explore implementing it in their infrastructure within 90 days.

case_studies.title: LLM-Assisted Dynamic Threat Analysis for Attacker-Reachable Software Weaknesses in Autonomous Vehicles
case_studies.abstract: Autonomous vehicles depend on large safety-critical software stacks, where weaknesses reachable from adversarial inputs may affect steering, braking, or other control decisions. Static analysis can identify candidate sites, but dynamically confirming exploitability requires executable test artifacts that are difficult to construct manually. We investigate whether large language models (LLMs) can automate this process for Autoware, an open-source autonomous-driving stack. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of identifying and confirming software weaknesses in autonomous vehicles by using large language models to automate dynamic threat analysis. The researchers built a system that uses LLMs to identify and test potential weaknesses in the Autoware open-source autonomous-driving stack. The result is a more efficient way to identify potential security threats in autonomous vehicle software.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for autonomous vehicle software development, here is what to do: review your static analysis processes, consider integrating large language models to automate dynamic threat analysis, and prioritize testing of identified weaknesses. This flags a risk: if your organization uses open-source autonomous-driving stacks like Autoware, check for similar weaknesses immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant for specialized fields like autonomous vehicle software development.

case_studies.title: Before You Say It: Anticipating Verbal Behavior from Longitudinal Everyday Conversations with LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Knowing someone deeply means not just understanding what they say or do but also how they will likely think, react, and engage across situations. Such predictions could eventually inform systems to anticipate when the individual is about to deviate from their goal, catch regrettable behaviors before they are made, and surface blind spots before they take hold. While many interactive systems model users to enable more personalized interactions, most cannot make such behavioral predictions, as this often requires longitudinal observation and inference of how the individual's behaviors unfold acr
case_studies.summary: This research aims to predict verbal behavior from everyday conversations, building a system that can anticipate actions and reactions. It built a model using longitudinal conversations with large language models to inform systems that can catch regrettable behaviors before they happen. The result is a predictive model that can surface blind spots before they take hold.

case_studies.title: VDGR-RAG: Vectors, Directories, Graphs, and Reflection Are All You Need for Unified Reasoning over Hierarchical Enterprise Knowledge
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is essential for enterprise knowledge question answering (QA), particularly in domains with complex product documentation like telecommunications. However, existing RAG approaches largely overlook the holistic integration of diverse retrieval strengths, leading to inaccurate domain routing, poor utilization of hierarchical document structures, and consequently limited reasoning capabilities over enterprise knowledge. To address these limitations, we present VDGR-RAG, which integrates vector retrieval, directory-driven reasoning, graph traversal, and iterati
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inaccurate domain routing and poor utilization of hierarchical document structures in enterprise knowledge question answering. The authors built VDGR-RAG, a unified reasoning model that integrates vector retrieval, directory-driven reasoning, graph traversal, and reflection. The result is improved reasoning capabilities over complex enterprise knowledge.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on enterprise knowledge question answering and natural language processing, rather than cloud infrastructure management.

case_studies.title: SAGE: SLO-Aware Adaptive Retrieval for Production RAG Systems
case_studies.abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems in production operate under strict service level objectives (SLOs) on tail latency and infrastructure cost. However, standard retrieval pipelines rely on fixed retrieval budgets that ignore query difficulty, over-retrieving for easy queries and under-serving hard ones, forcing operators to trade answer quality against SLO compliance. This paper proposes SAGE, a learned SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that dynamically selects the number of passages k per query. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of optimizing retrieval pipelines in production Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems to meet service level objectives (SLOs) while improving answer quality. The researchers built SAGE, a learned SLO-aware adaptive retrieval policy that dynamically adjusts the number of passages retrieved per query. The result is improved SLO compliance and answer quality without increased infrastructure cost.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage RAG systems, here is what to do: review your current retrieval pipeline configuration, consider implementing SAGE or a similar adaptive retrieval policy to optimize query performance and SLO compliance. This flags a risk: if your org uses fixed retrieval budgets, check your SLO compliance and answer quality immediately to avoid potential issues. Apply SAGE to dynamically adjust retrieval budgets and improve overall system performance.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper proposes a retrieval policy for RAG systems in production, focusing on SLAs and query difficulty. However, it lacks a clear IT angle and direct relevance to IT engineers' work.
